A greedy algorithm makes locally optimal choices at each step, hoping or proving that these choices lead to a globally optimal solution. Unlike divide and conquer or dynamic programming, greedy algorithms commit to decisions immediately without reconsidering them later. They are often fast and simple to implement but don't always work correctly. The challenge is proving or identifying when a greedy approach guarantees optimality.

The core idea is straightforward. At each step, select the option that seems best right now without looking ahead. Once a choice is made, it's never undone or reconsidered. There's no backtracking. Greedy algorithms are naturally iterative and typically run in O of n log n or O of n time.

Greedy works under specific conditions. Matroid structures are certain optimization problems with the greedy choice property—a locally optimal choice is part of a globally optimal solution. Optimal substructure means the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. When both properties hold, greedy is provably correct. When they don't, greedy may fail.

Classic examples show greedy at its best. Activity selection schedules non-overlapping tasks by greedily picking the earliest-ending activity first. Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix-free code by repeatedly merging the lowest-frequency nodes. Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm greedily explores the nearest unvisited node and is optimal for non-negative weights. The fractional knapsack problem can be solved greedily by stuffing items in order of highest value-to-weight ratio. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree adds the lowest-weight edge that doesn't create a cycle.

But greedy fails on some important problems. The zero-one knapsack problem can't break items, so greedy by value-to-weight ratio doesn't work optimally. You need dynamic programming instead. The traveling salesman problem solved greedily as nearest-neighbor is fast but suboptimal. Many graph coloring and scheduling variants have no greedy solution.

The strategy for analyzing whether greedy works is the exchange argument. You prove correctness by showing that any non-greedy solution can be transformed into a greedy solution without worsening optimality. When greedy fails, you provide counterexamples and verify with dynamic programming or branch-and-bound algorithms instead.

Greedy algorithms are a programmer's workhorse. They're simple to code, fast to execute, and excellent for approximation when true optimality is intractable or infeasible. They dominate practical applications in networking, resource allocation, and scheduling. But the trap is assuming greedy works without proof. A hallmark of algorithmic maturity is recognizing the class of problems where greedy is valid and having the discipline to reach for dynamic programming or approximation techniques when it isn't. Many interview problems test exactly this discernment. Greedy algorithms are a major algorithm design paradigm. Divide and conquer is an alternative approach that's usually slower but more general. Dynamic programming succeeds when greedy fails, using exhaustive cached search. Many greedy algorithms operate on graphs, like Dijkstra and Kruskal. And greedy algorithms typically have favorable complexity bounds expressed in Big O notation.
